passage:
Thursday night. The maths test was today. Halfway through I could not remember the formula, and I saw Kiran's paper on the next bench, and I looked. Once, then twice. Nobody saw. The invigilator was at the window. I got the answer and moved on. I should feel relieved. Instead my stomach has been twisted since eleven this morning. All evening I kept hearing Papa: "A low mark is fine. A false mark is not." Nobody will ever know, and that is exactly what bothers me. It is my paper and it isn't true.
Tomorrow I will tell Ma'am and ask if I can retake it, even if my marks drop. I am scared, but I would rather be scared than carry this.
Madhav

qa.a: Papa would probably respect it, since Madhav remembers Papa saying a low mark is fine but a false mark is not.

passage:
Wednesday
In today's maths test I looked at Tanvir's paper. Only for question 7. He didn't know. Ma'am didn't see. Nobody saw.
I got full marks. I should feel happy.
I feel sick instead. At lunch, Tanvir said, "You got 20 too? Nice!" and I couldn't look at him.
Mumma always says, "Don't do anything that brings shame on the family." But nobody knows. There's no shame. So why do I feel like this?
I think it's because I know. I'm the one who has to be the person who copied. That's worse than anyone finding out.
Tomorrow I'm going to tell Ma'am I copied question 7. She can cut the marks. I'd rather have 16 and be able to look at Tanvir.
Shreya

passage:
In the village school near Satna, the Class 9 half-yearly exam was held in the veranda because the classroom roof was leaking. Gautam, fifteen, sat near the pillar. A folded chit blew against his foot, answers for the science section. He glanced at it. Just once.
He wrote two answers from it. The invigilator was busy with a crying younger child and never saw.
That evening, Gautam couldn't eat. His mother asked what was wrong. "Nothing," he said. But all night he kept seeing Anjali Madam's face, the teacher who'd stayed after school to teach him the same chapter.
The next morning, he waited outside the staffroom. "Madam, I used a chit for two answers. Nobody saw. But I did."
Anjali Madam looked at him for a long moment. "That took courage. We'll cut those marks. And we'll go over that chapter again, together."

qa.q: Where was the exam held, and why?
qa.a: It was held in the veranda because the classroom roof was leaking.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling when he couldn't eat?
qa.a: Gautam felt guilty, thinking of Anjali Madam, who had stayed after school to teach him, even though nobody saw him cheat.

qa.q: How did Anjali Madam respond well to Gautam's confession?
qa.a: She praised his courage, gave a fair consequence by cutting the marks, and offered to reteach the chapter, supporting his conscience.

qa.q: How might Anjali Madam feel after Gautam's confession?
qa.a: Anjali Madam probably feels a little disappointed but also proud and touched that he chose honesty.

grounding: In a village school, a teenager feels guilt after cheating unseen, because it clashes with his values, and confesses.

passage: During the Friday vocabulary quiz in Montreal, Mr. Gagnon stepped out to answer the door, and Nour saw Paulo's paper lying right there, the answer to number seven in neat blue ink. She copied it. Nobody saw. She got twenty out of twenty, a first. All weekend the score sat in her stomach like a stone. At Sunday dinner her grandmother, who had grown up in a village where everyone watched everyone, told a story about her own school: "We feared the neighbours finding out. But the worst was when I knew and no one else did." On Monday Nour waited after class. "Number seven wasn't mine," she told Mr. Gagnon. He looked at her for a moment. "Thank you for telling me. Take the quiz again at lunch." She got eighteen. It felt lighter.

qa.a: She got eighteen.

qa.q: Why did the perfect score feel like a stone in Nour's stomach?
qa.a: Nour felt guilty because copying clashed with her own values, even though nobody had seen.

qa.a: He probably respects her more for confessing something nobody saw, and trusts her conscience.
